Bauhaus. The name means Building House, and it was a German design school and movement from nineteen nineteen to nineteen thirty three that unified art, craft, and industrial design under a single philosophy: function, form, and beauty are inseparable. Founded by architect Walter Gropius, it integrated painting, sculpture, typography, and architecture while emphasizing honest materials, geometric simplicity, and the notion that good design democratizes beauty by making it accessible through mass production.

Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar, Germany, in nineteen nineteen, and he assembled a faculty of avant-garde artists including Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, and László Moholy-Nagy. This brought together some of Europe's most innovative minds under one roof. The core principle was that form follows function—objects should be designed from their purpose outward, free from applied ornament, celebrating the inherent beauty of material and construction.

The school integrated color theory through Kandinsky, geometric composition through Klee, and typography through Herbert Bayer into a systematic pedagogy taught through studios and workshops. The practical output was remarkable. Bauhaus produced influential graphic design, furniture like Marcel Breuer's tubular steel chairs, pottery, textiles, and architectural principles that became foundational to modernism itself.

The school relocated from Weimar to Dessau in nineteen twenty five, then to Berlin in nineteen thirty two, operating under increasing political pressure as the political climate shifted. The Nazi regime closed Bauhaus in nineteen thirty three, designating it as degenerate. But the movement's influence could not be destroyed so easily.

Faculty and students emigrated globally after the closure, spreading Bauhaus principles to America and throughout the world. Its influence on twentieth-century design remains immeasurable and foundational.
